## One page, six decisions

[The prospectus]{.eyebrow}

- Next week you hand in one page saying what you are studying, why it matters, and how you
  will do it
- It is not busywork. It is a **diagnostic**.
- If you cannot state the project clearly on one page, you do not yet understand it well
  enough to start, and better to find that out now than in November
- The model prospectus in Chapter 6 runs about 250 words
- You leave today knowing which of the six pieces you cannot yet write

## The six components

| Component | Length |
|---|---|
| Descriptive title hinting at key variables | one line |
| Research questions or hypotheses | 1 to 3, not 10 |
| Theoretical framework | 2 to 3 sentences |
| Gap in the literature | 2 to 3 sentences |
| Method overview | 3 to 4 sentences |
| Expected contribution | 1 to 2 sentences |

## Title and question

From the model prospectus:

- **Title.** "Directed and broadcast chat in gaming and non-gaming streams: A content
  analysis of the Twitch working corpus."
- **RQ.** "Does the proportion of chat messages directed at the streamer differ between
  gaming and non-gaming streams, among the 50 channels in the working corpus?"

The title names the variables. The question names the comparison. Between them they have
already ruled out most of what you could have done, which is the point.

## Framework and gap

- **Framework.** Uses and gratifications (Katz, Blumler, & Gurevitch, 1973): audiences
  actively select media to satisfy needs, including social ones
- If viewing is socially motivated, *how* viewers participate is one observable trace of
  the gratification they are seeking
- **Gap.** Livestreaming motivation research is dominated by self-report surveys
  (Sjöblom & Hamari, 2017; Hilvert-Bruce et al., 2018)
- Whether the behavioural traces in a chat log back those surveys up is largely unexamined

## Method, in four sentences

- A **stratified sample of 1,500 chat messages** from the 50-channel working corpus,
  balanced across gaming and non-gaming
- **Unit of analysis:** each message
- **Coding:** directed at the streamer, broadcast to the room, or unclassifiable
- **Reliability:** a second coder on a 10 percent subsample, Krippendorff's alpha
- Then the proportion of directed messages gets compared between the two groups

## Your turn {.discuss}

- In your project, what is the single **comparison** you will make? Say it as "X will be
  compared between A and B."
- What is your unit of analysis: a message, a stream, a channel, an hour?
- Which of the six components do you currently have nothing at all to write?

*Two minutes. The component you cannot fill is your homework, and we will hear a few.*

## Same data, different theory

Swap the lens and everything downstream of it changes:

- **Title.** Markers of parasocial bond in viewer chat, large-audience versus
  small-audience streams
- **RQ.** Do smaller-audience streams show a higher rate of parasocial language?
- **Framework.** Parasocial interaction (Horton & Wohl, 1956); Hilvert-Bruce et al. (2018)
  found smaller-channel viewers more socially motivated

Same corpus. Different study entirely.

## The second method paragraph

- **1,000 messages**, split between top-quartile and bottom-quartile channels by average
  viewer count
- **Three markers** coded present or absent: second-person address, expressions of
  familiarity, emotional disclosure
- Reliability on a 10 percent subsample, Krippendorff's alpha
- The rate of each marker compared between the two audience-size groups

## Pick the workload, not just the question

- The first prospectus codes **one** variable. The second codes **three**.
- Three variables means three codebook decisions, three reliability checks, three sets of
  results, and roughly three times the coding hours
- The second is the better study to read and the heavier term to survive
- Neither is more correct. Both are defensible plans.
- Make that trade visible now, while it is still a paragraph, rather than halfway through
  coding in November

## What you do not need yet

- The prospectus is **pre-statistics work**
- You do not need to know which test you will run, or what your *p*-value is, or any R code
- "Will be compared" is genuinely all the method paragraph needs at this stage
- What you commit to is structure: question, theory, unit of analysis, coding scheme,
  comparison
- If you have been putting this off because you thought you needed the statistics first,
  you do not

## A prospectus that fails

> **Title.** Twitch and Society.
>
> **RQ.** How does Twitch chat affect viewers' sense of community, and what is the role of
> parasocial relationships and social identity across different streams and genres? Also,
> are streamers becoming more popular over time?
>
> **Framework.** Parasocial interaction, social identity, and political economy.
>
> **Method.** I will look at some chat logs and see what patterns emerge.

## Why it fails

- The title names **no variables**
- The research question is three or four questions stacked on top of each other
- Three theories pull in different directions and cannot all be operationalized on this data
- The method cannot be judged for feasibility, because nothing in it is specific
- The contribution could be pasted into any project

That draft was not lazy. It was trying to do too much, which is what ambition looks like
before it gets disciplined.

## The feasibility test

Before you submit, answer four questions honestly:

- **Can you get the data?** Here, yes: the working corpus ships inside the `v2v` package
- **Can you analyze it in the time you have?** Fifty channels is manageable. The full 1,690
  is not, for one person in one term.
- **Does your method match your question?** Content analysis tells you what is in the
  content, never why a viewer felt something
- **Have you controlled scope creep?** Narrow until it hurts slightly, then narrow again

## The prospectus as pre-registration

- **Pre-registration** means publicly committing to your hypotheses, methods, and analysis
  plan before you collect or analyze anything
- Services like the Open Science Framework timestamp that commitment so it cannot move
- Simmons, Nelson, and Simonsohn (2011) showed that without a fixed plan, researchers
  adjust hypotheses and variables until something crosses significance
- That is where the phrase **researcher degrees of freedom** comes from
- Pre-registration closes them by making the plan inspectable by somebody else

## Your prospectus is your record

- It documents what you planned before you had coded or analyzed anything
- When you are later tempted to add a variable or chase a surprise, it is the record of
  what you actually set out to do
- A difference between the plan and the paper is not automatically wrong. It is **visible**,
  and it raises a question worth raising.
- This is Chapter 2's transparency argument, pointed at your own project
